chunks.content: Diabetes - type 1: What are the causes and risk factors? Type 1 diabetes is caused by an absolute insulin deficiency, usually resulting from autoimmune destruction of the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. Risk factors include: Genetic factors — type 1 diabetes is a heritable polygenic disease. A sibling of a person with type 1 diabetes has 6–7% risk of developing it themselves. This risk increases to 30–70% in identical twins. The risk for a child is 1–9% if a parent has type 1 diabetes.

A sibling of a person with type 1 diabetes has 6–7% risk of developing it themselves. This risk increases to 30–70% in identical twins. The risk for a child is 1–9% if a parent has type 1 diabetes. Several different alleles (alternative forms of a gene) and haplotypes (combinations of alleles) have been associated with either an increased or decreased risk of type 1 diabetes. However, the mechanisms by which these haplotypes interact and alter risk are not completely understood. Environmental factors — there is evidence that in genetically susceptible people, certain environmental factors can trigger the development of autoimmunity to the pancreatic beta cells. Environmental factors associated with type 1 diabetes include diet, vitamin D exposure, obesity, early-life exposure to viruses associated with islet inflammation (such as enteroviruses), and decreased gut-microbiome diversity.

The importance of environmental risk factors (regardless of genetic background risk) are highlighted by the large differences in the incidence of type 1 diabetes in genetically similar populations that are separated by socioeconomic borders and by the increasing incidence of type 1 diabetes in genetically low-risk people.
